title: Historical Ecosystems and Fire Return Intervals
text:
LANDFIRE’s Biophysical Settings (BpSs) are the source data for the maps and charts below.

BpS models represent the vegetation system that may have been dominant on the landscape prior to Euro-American settlement. These models are based on a combination of the current environment and an approximation of the historical disturbance regime. Read more.

Check out this 3-minute tutorial for a quick refresher on the basics of Biophysical Settings Models.
Use this page as a starting point to explore the most prevalent BpSs for your analysis area. In addition to the charts and maps, the historical disturbance data can be directly accessed using this site.

title: Vegetation Departure
text:
Using LANDFIRE’s Biophysical Settings spatial data to essentially map ‘ecosystem habitats’ and state-and-transition models to estimate the expected historical amounts of their succession classes we can estimate reference conditions under natural disturbance regimes. We can then quantify current succession class amounts with LANDFIRE’s succession class data. Below are succession class charts that allow for an exploration of which classes are over or under represented.
LANDFIRE’s Succession Classes Product:

characterizes current vegetation conditions with respect to the vegetation species composition (leaf-form and life-form, primarily), cover, and height ranges of the successional states that occur within each Biophysical Settings (BPS). SClass can also represent uncharacteristic vegetation components, including exotic species, tree plantations, canopy cover, etc. These components are not found within the compositional or structural variability of successional states defined for a BPS. Read more.

title: About this Project
text:
LANDFIRE (Landscape Fire and Resource Management Planning Tools) is a shared program between the U.S. Department of Agriculture Forest Service Fire and Aviation branch and the U.S. Department of the Interior. LANDFIRE provides 25+ national landscape-scale geo-spatial products, 950 vegetation models, and a suite of tools that support all-lands planning, management, and operations. Included in the product suite are current and historic conditions including ecosystem dynamic models that can be used for conservation, fire planning, and landscape management decisions.
The Nature Conservancy (TNC) is a Major Partner in the LANDFIRE Program supported by a cooperative agreement through USDA Forest Service. TNC’s LANDFIRE Team works closely with the LANDFIRE Business Leads, program staff, and other partners to provide support to LANDFIRE and the user community by:

Helping users understand the strengths, weaknesses, and appropriate uses of LANDFIRE products.
Locating, obtaining, and using geospatial data, tools, and models for fire and natural resource management, planning, and implementation.
Identifying and comparing management priorities, evaluating threats to ecosystems, and exploring outcomes under alternative management scenarios.


TNC’s LANDFIRE Team is advancing conservation outcomes through collaborative ecosystem science by supporting LANDFIRE users as they locate, obtain and apply the diverse suite of LANDFIRE products and data.

Created by TNC Ecologist, Randy Swaty, this preliminary landscape assessment leverages LANDFIRE’s unique geospatial products to advance beneficial outcomes for the wildland fire and natural resource communities. The central data in each project are created and managed by the cooperative inter-agency/inter-organizational LANDFIRE program.
These charts, maps, and graphs are based on current LANDFIRE products, and provide a starting point for further analysis. All maps, input datasets and further assistance can be obtained by contacting the author, Randy Swaty.
Substantial code contributions for GIS data processing by Myles Walimaa.

title: About this Project
text:
Biophysical Settings Products
A Biophysical Setting (BpS) is a concept that represents the vegetation that may have been dominant on the landscape prior to European colonization of North America and is based on both the current biophysical environment and an approximation of the historical disturbance regime.

LANDFIRE collaborated with experts around the country to create a description and model for every BpS in the US. Find BpS descriptions for your area here.
Check out the vegetation modeling website to learn how to integrate BpS into your work.
Read Blankenship et al. (2021) to learn how the models and descriptions were developed.

title: About this Project
text:
Vegetation Products
LANDFIRE (LF) existing vegetation layers describe the following elements: Existing Vegetation Type (EVT), Existing Vegetation Canopy Cover (EVC), and Existing Vegetation Height (EVH). These layers are created using predictive landscape models based on extensive field-referenced data, satellite imagery and biophysical gradient layers using classification and regression trees.

title: Smoothed Biophysical Settings polygons in ArcGIS Pro
text:
A protocol for turning a 30 m LANDFIRE Biophysical Settings (BpS) raster into rounded, natural-looking polygons for one or more groups of BpSs, for any area of interest. The same steps work for any categorical raster (e.g., Existing Vegetation Type) by swapping the field used to define groups.


Converting a classified raster directly to polygons (Raster to Polygon) traces pixel edges, so polygons come out stair-stepped, with thousands of tiny slivers. Smoothing the polygons afterwards (Smooth Polygon) softens corners but keeps every speck. This protocol smooths the raster first, then contours it:

For each group, make a 1/0 raster (1 = pixel belongs to the group).
Average it to a coarser cell size, so each cell holds the group’s share of that cell.
Blur that share with a moving-window average, so each cell holds the group’s share of its neighborhood.
Draw the contour at a chosen share (e.g., 40%), and keep the area above it.

Contour lines are interpolated between cell centers, so the polygons are naturally rounded. The amount of blur controls how much detail is kept; the contour level controls how inclusive the polygons are.
This is a form of cartographic generalization: deliberately simplifying a map to suit its scale and purpose. In effect, step 3 is a moving-window proportion of the group (the same idea as a kernel density surface), and step 4 traces an isoline of that surface, much like drawing an elevation contour on a DEM. See Learn more for background on each piece.



Starting values that worked well on a ~1.5 million acre national forest. Adjust them to your landscape and map scale (see Tuning).








Setting
Starting value
Effect




Aggregation
3 × 3 cells (30 m → 90 m), mean
Speeds processing; each cell = share of group


Blur
3 × 3 cell mean, one pass
More passes = rounder, less detail


Contour level
0.4 (40% neighborhood share)
Lower = more inclusive, picks up narrow strips


Fill holes smaller than
40 acres
Removes pinholes


Simplify tolerance
15 m (Douglas-Peucker)
Thins vertices for web maps


Minimum polygon size
20 acres
Drops small patches






Decide which BpSs to map and how to group them. A group can be a single BpS or several related ones (e.g., all spruce-fir variants). For each group, record:

Group name
BPS_CODE values in the group. Use BPS_CODE, not the raster VALUE: one BpS code can have several raster values (map zone variants), and the group should include all of them. Step 2 explains how to find the codes. Read the BpS model descriptions to decide which BpSs belong together.
Priority, if mapping more than one group. Groups are smoothed independently, so their edges can overlap; overlaps go to the higher-priority group (step 9). Putting rarer or more important groups first keeps them from being swallowed by widespread neighbors.
Color. The colorblind-safe Okabe-Ito palette works well: #0072B2, #F0E442, #56B4E9, #009E73, #CC79A7, #E69F00, #D55E00, #000000. Leave a few colors unused if other layers will be drawn on top.

A worksheet like this keeps things straight. Number the groups by priority; that number (g1, g2, …) is used in every output name.



Priority
Group
BPS_CODE values
Color




1
Group A
code, code, …
#0072B2


2
Group B
code
#009E73


…










ArcGIS Pro with the Spatial Analyst extension (Aggregate, Focal Statistics, Contour, Lookup, Tabulate Area).
A BpS raster covering the area of interest, with its attribute table (BPS_CODE field). Download from landfire.gov (e.g., via the LANDFIRE viewer).
An area-of-interest boundary polygon.





Create a project. Open ArcGIS Pro and start a new project from the Map template. Pro creates a project file geodatabase (YourProject.gdb). Save every output there unless told otherwise; geodatabases handle long field names and large polygons better than shapefiles.
Add data. On the Map tab, click Add Data and add the BpS raster and the boundary polygon.
Check the BpS attribute table. In the Contents pane, right-click the BpS raster and choose Attribute Table. You should see VALUE, BPS_CODE, BPS_NAME and other fields. If only VALUE and COUNT are present, the attributes were lost (this can happen after clipping). Use Join Field to bring them back from the CSV attribute table that comes with the LANDFIRE download, joining on VALUE.
Trim the raster if it is much larger than your area. If the BpS raster covers a whole region or the country, use Clip Raster to cut it to your boundary’s extent plus a buffer of about 1 km. The buffer lets polygons at the edge “see” real neighbors during the blur; the polygons are clipped to the exact boundary later (step 7).
Set environments. On the Analysis tab, click Environments and set:

Output Coordinate System: a projected system in meters. Choosing Same as Input with the BpS raster’s projection (NAD 1983 Contiguous USA Albers, EPSG 5070, for CONUS LANDFIRE) works. Avoid geographic (degrees) coordinates; areas and distances would be wrong.
Processing Extent: same as the BpS raster.
Snap Raster: the BpS raster. This keeps every raster output aligned to the same grid.
Leave Mask empty. Cells outside the boundary need to be 0, not NoData, for the blur (handled in step 3).

See Geoprocessing environment settings for details.




Open a tool: on the Analysis tab, click Tools. In the Geoprocessing pane, search for the tool by name, fill in the parameters and click Run.
Check results: a green banner means success. Click View Details to see warnings; some are harmless, but read them.
Rerun with different inputs: on the Analysis tab, click History. Double-click a previous run to reopen the tool with the same settings, then change the inputs and output names. This is the fastest way to repeat steps 2–8 for each group (Geoprocessing history).
Automating: steps 2–8 can be chained in ModelBuilder, with the group codes and name as model parameters. Steps 9 and 11 include Python you can paste into the Python window (Analysis tab > Python > Python Window).





Steps 2–8 are run once per group. Names below use gX for the group’s priority number (g1, g2, …), so gX_mask means g1_mask for the first group, g2_mask for the second, and so on.


The BpS raster’s cell values are VALUE codes; we want cells to hold BPS_CODE instead, so a group can be selected by code.
Lookup (Spatial Analyst)

Input raster: BpS raster
Lookup field: BPS_CODE
Output raster: bps_code

Check: click a few cells with the Explore tool. The pop-up value should be a 5-digit code (e.g., 13022) that matches BPS_CODE for that pixel in the BpS raster.



Find the group’s codes.

Open the BpS raster’s attribute table.
Click Select By Attributes and build a query on BPS_NAME, e.g., BPS_NAME contains the text Spruce.
Note the distinct BPS_CODE values among the selected rows. Several rows may share one code; list each code once.
Record the codes in your worksheet.

Make the mask with Raster Calculator (Spatial Analyst), using Con and InList. Double-click bps_code in the Rasters list to insert it, then type the rest:
Con(InList("bps_code", [13651, 13652, 13653]), 1, 0)
Replace the codes with your group’s codes.

Output raster: gX_mask

Cells outside the BpS raster’s data area stay NoData; that is expected.
If InList is unavailable in your version, use Con(("bps_code" == 13651) | ("bps_code" == 13652), 1, 0), or Reclassify the group’s codes to 1 and all other codes to 0.
Check: symbolize gX_mask with Unique Values (1 in a bright color, 0 with no color). The 1s should match the group’s pixels in the BpS raster.



Aggregating converts 1/0 pixels into a share. For example, a 90 m cell containing 4 group pixels out of 9 gets a value of 0.44.
Aggregate (Spatial Analyst; see How Aggregate works)

Input raster: gX_mask
Output raster: gX_share
Cell factor: 3
Aggregation technique: Mean
Expand extent if needed: checked
Ignore NoData in calculations: checked (cells at the edge average only their valid pixels)

Then Raster Calculator:
Con(IsNull("gX_share"), 0, "gX_share")

Output raster: gX_sharez

Check: the output is floating point, ranging from 0 to 1, with a 90 m cell size (Properties > Source > Raster Information).



Each cell gets the average of itself and its 8 neighbors, so it now holds the group’s share of a 270 m × 270 m neighborhood.
Focal Statistics (Spatial Analyst; see How Focal Statistics works)

Input raster: gX_sharez
Output raster: gX_smooth
Neighborhood: Rectangle
Height: 3, Width: 3, Units type: Cell
Statistics type: Mean
Ignore NoData in calculations: checked

Check: values still range from 0 to 1, and the surface looks like a soft-focus version of gX_sharez.
Optional: extra passes. For rounder, simpler polygons, run Focal Statistics again with the same settings on gX_smooth, then contour that output instead. Each pass blurs a little more. Repeated averaging approaches a Gaussian blur; with 90 m cells, one pass blurs by about 73 m, two passes by about 104 m and three by about 127 m. One pass works well for most uses. When tested on a 1.5 million acre forest, two passes cut the polygon count by about 20% and changed total acres by less than 1%.



Contour (Spatial Analyst; see How Contouring works)

Input raster: gX_smooth
Output feature class: gX_bands
Contour interval: your contour level (e.g., 0.4)
Base contour: 0
Contour type: Contour polygon

The output is a set of non-overlapping bands: 0–0.4, 0.4–0.8 and 0.8 up to the maximum. Setting the interval equal to the level guarantees a band boundary exactly at the level.
Keep the bands at or above the level:

Open the attribute table of gX_bands. It has fields holding each band’s lower and upper contour values; field names vary by Pro version.
Select Layer By Attribute: new selection, where the lower-value field is greater than or equal to 0.399. The 0.399 allows for values stored as 0.39999999.
Pairwise Dissolve with the selection active (only selected features are used):

Input features: gX_bands
Output feature class: gX_contour
Dissolve fields: none
Create multipart features: checked

This merges the selected bands into one feature: everywhere the neighborhood share is at least the level.

Alternative: Contour shell up returns overlapping “shells”, each running from a contour value up to the raster maximum. Keep the shell whose lower value equals your level, and delete the rest.
Check: symbolize gX_smooth with two classes, breaking at the contour level, and overlay gX_contour as a hollow outline. The outline should trace the class break, with the high class inside.



Eliminate Polygon Part (Data Management)

Input features: gX_contour
Output feature class: gX_filled
Condition: Area
Area: e.g., 40 Acres
Eliminate contained parts only: checked (removes holes only; outer polygons of any size are kept)




Pairwise Clip (Analysis)

Input features: gX_filled
Clip features: area-of-interest boundary
Output feature class: gX_clip

Then Multipart To Singlepart (Data Management), so each separate patch becomes its own feature:

Input features: gX_clip
Output feature class: gX_single




Simplify Polygon (Cartography; see How Simplify Line and Simplify Polygon work)

Input features: gX_single
Output feature class: gX_simple
Simplification algorithm: Retain critical points (Douglas-Peucker)
Simplification tolerance: e.g., 15 Meters
Minimum area: 0
Handling topological errors: Resolve topological errors (keeps edges from crossing)
Keep collapsed points: unchecked

Contours have a vertex every few meters; simplifying removes most of them without visibly changing the shape.
Label the group. Use Add Field and Calculate Field on gX_simple to add:








Field
Type
Calculate Field expression (Python)




group
Text (length 100)
"Group A" (your group name, in quotes)


priority
Short
1 (your group’s priority number)



Repeat steps 2–8 for each group. With only one group, skip step 9 and use g1_simple as the input to step 10.



The problem. Each group was smoothed on its own, so in mixed areas two groups can both pass the 40% contour and their polygons overlap. Picture a strip where pine and hemlock pixels are interspersed: after smoothing, the pine polygon and the hemlock polygon both cover the strip. If both were mapped, that strip would be counted twice in acreage totals, and the map would show two colors stacked on each other.
The rule. Each overlap goes to the higher-priority group. For each group, erase every area already covered by any higher-priority group. Group 1 keeps everything; group 2 loses what overlaps group 1; group 3 loses what overlaps groups 1 or 2; and so on.
Worked example for four groups:



Group
Build the erase layer with Merge
Pairwise Erase input
Erase features
Output




g1
(none: use Copy Features to copy g1_simple)


g1_final


g2
(none: one layer)
g2_simple
g1_simple
g2_final


g3
g1_simple + g2_simple → above_g3
g3_simple
above_g3
g3_final


g4
g1_simple + g2_simple + g3_simple → above_g4
g4_simple
above_g4
g4_final



Erasing with the _simple layers (before erase) gives the same result as erasing with the _final layers: together, groups 1 and 2 cover the same ground either way.
Click by click (group 3 shown; repeat for each group from priority 2 down):

Open Merge (Data Management).

Input datasets: add g1_simple and g2_simple (every group with a higher priority than the one you’re processing)
Output dataset: above_g3
Leave the field map as is; the fields don’t matter for erasing.

The merged layer may contain overlapping polygons; that’s fine.
Open Pairwise Erase (Analysis).

Input features: g3_simple
Erase features: above_g3
Output feature class: g3_final

Every part of g3_simple that falls inside above_g3 is removed; everything else is copied with its attributes.

For group 2, skip the Merge and erase with g1_simple directly. For group 1, run Copy Features from g1_simple to g1_final.
Because the erasing edges are themselves smooth contours, the cut edges stay rounded.
Or run it in the Python window. This does the whole step for any number of groups. Edit the two lines marked EDIT:
import arcpy

arcpy.env.workspace = r"C:\path\to\YourProject.gdb"  # EDIT: geodatabase with the gX_simple layers
arcpy.env.overwriteOutput = True

# EDIT: one entry per group, highest priority first
simple = ["g1_simple", "g2_simple", "g3_simple", "g4_simple"]

for k, fc in enumerate(simple, start=1):
    out = f"g{k}_final"
    if k == 1:
        arcpy.management.CopyFeatures(fc, out)
    elif k == 2:
        arcpy.analysis.PairwiseErase(fc, simple[0], out)
    else:
        above = f"above_g{k}"
        arcpy.management.Merge(simple[:k - 1], above)
        arcpy.analysis.PairwiseErase(fc, above, out)
    print(out, arcpy.management.GetCount(out)[0], "polygons")
Check:

Visual: turn on g1_simple and g2_simple and find a place where they overlap. Then turn on g1_final and g2_final in the same place: g2_final should have a gap exactly where g1_final sits.
Area: each gX_final should have the same or less area than its gX_simple. The difference is the overlap it gave up.
No overlaps remain: run Count Overlapping Features (Analysis) with all gX_final layers as inputs and Minimum Overlap Count set to 2. The output should be empty, or contain only slivers of a few square meters from coordinate rounding.





Merge (Data Management)

Input datasets: all gX_final layers
Output dataset: bps_smooth_all
The group and priority fields match in every input, so the default field map keeps them.

Smoothed polygons absorb some neighboring BpSs at their edges. Two attributes describe how “pure” each polygon is:

purity: the share of the polygon’s area made up of its own group’s BpSs (0 to 1).
main_bps: the group’s BPS_CODE with the most area in the polygon. This is useful for groups with several BpSs.

Both come from Tabulate Area (Spatial Analyst), which measures how much of each BPS_CODE falls in each polygon:

Input raster or feature zone data: bps_smooth
Zone field: poly_id
Input raster or feature class data: bps_code (from step 1)
Class field: Value
Output table: tab_bps
Processing cell size: 30

The output table has one row per polygon and one field per BPS_CODE, named VALUE_<code> (e.g., VALUE_13022), holding area in square meters.
Turning that table into purity and main BpS by hand is tedious, so paste this into the Python window. Edit the three EDIT lines; the group names must match the group field exactly.
import arcpy
arcpy.CheckOutExtension("Spatial")

arcpy.env.workspace = r"C:\path\to\YourProject.gdb"  # EDIT
polys = "bps_smooth"
groups = {                                            # EDIT: group name -> its BPS_CODEs
    "Group A": [13651, 13652, 13653],
    "Group B": [13622],
}
cell_size = 30                                        # EDIT if your BpS raster is not 30 m

arcpy.sa.TabulateArea(polys, "poly_id", "bps_code", "Value", "tab_bps", cell_size)

tab_fields = [f.name for f in arcpy.ListFields("tab_bps")]
zone_field = next(f for f in tab_fields if f.lower() == "poly_id")
code_fields = [f for f in tab_fields if f.upper().startswith("VALUE_")]

areas = {}
with arcpy.da.SearchCursor("tab_bps", [zone_field] + code_fields) as cur:
    for row in cur:
        areas[row[0]] = {int(f.split("_")[1]): (v or 0) for f, v in zip(code_fields, row[1:])}

existing = [f.name for f in arcpy.ListFields(polys)]
for name, ftype in [("main_bps", "LONG"), ("purity", "DOUBLE")]:
    if name not in existing:
        arcpy.management.AddField(polys, name, ftype)

with arcpy.da.UpdateCursor(polys, ["poly_id", "group", "main_bps", "purity"]) as cur:
    for pid, grp, _, _ in cur:
        a = areas.get(pid, {})
        own = {code: a.get(code, 0) for code in groups[grp]}
        total = sum(a.values())
        main = max(own, key=own.get)
        purity = sum(own.values()) / total if total else None
        cur.updateRow([pid, grp, main, purity])

print("done")

Join table: the BpS raster, Join table field: BPS_CODE
Transfer fields: BPS_NAME

How to read the ratio of smoothed to raw acres:

Roughly 90–110%: typical for widespread groups that occur in large patches.
Well above 100%: the contour is absorbing neighboring types in mixed areas. Raise the contour level.
Well below 100%: the group occurs as small or scattered patches that fall below the contour level or the minimum size. Lower the contour level or the minimum size, if those patches matter.

Overlaps: see the check at the end of step 9.





Rounder, simpler shapes: add a second or third blur pass (step 4).
Capture narrow or scattered patches: lower the contour level (e.g., 0.35). Expect polygons to grow into neighboring types.
Group-specific settings: each group can use its own contour level or number of passes. Scattered types benefit from a lower contour level and a single pass.
Map scale:

Small areas or large-scale maps: use a smaller minimum size, and possibly no aggregation (cell factor 1, so the blur works on 30 m cells; slower).
Regional extents: use a larger aggregation factor or more blur passes.

Simplify tolerance: keep it well below the cell size so shapes stay rounded. Increase it only if file size matters (e.g., web maps).

title: Smoothed Biophysical Settings polygons in ArcGIS Pro
text:
Converting a classified raster directly to polygons (Raster to Polygon) traces pixel edges, so polygons come out stair-stepped, with thousands of tiny slivers. Smoothing the polygons afterwards (Smooth Polygon) softens corners but keeps every speck. This protocol smooths the raster first, then contours it:

For each group, make a 1/0 raster (1 = pixel belongs to the group).
Average it to a coarser cell size, so each cell holds the group’s share of that cell.
Blur that share with a moving-window average, so each cell holds the group’s share of its neighborhood.
Draw the contour at a chosen share (e.g., 40%), and keep the area above it.

Contour lines are interpolated between cell centers, so the polygons are naturally rounded. The amount of blur controls how much detail is kept; the contour level controls how inclusive the polygons are.
This is a form of cartographic generalization: deliberately simplifying a map to suit its scale and purpose. In effect, step 3 is a moving-window proportion of the group (the same idea as a kernel density surface), and step 4 traces an isoline of that surface, much like drawing an elevation contour on a DEM. See Learn more for background on each piece.

title: Smoothed Biophysical Settings polygons in ArcGIS Pro
text:
Set these once for the project (Analysis > Environments) before running any tools:

title: Smoothed Biophysical Settings polygons in ArcGIS Pro
text:
Steps 2–8 are run once per group. Names below use gX for the group’s priority number (g1, g2, …), so gX_mask means g1_mask for the first group, g2_mask for the second, and so on.


The BpS raster’s cell values are VALUE codes; we want cells to hold BPS_CODE instead, so a group can be selected by code.
Lookup (Spatial Analyst)

Input raster: BpS raster
Lookup field: BPS_CODE
Output raster: bps_code

Check: click a few cells with the Explore tool. The pop-up value should be a 5-digit code (e.g., 13022) that matches BPS_CODE for that pixel in the BpS raster.



Find the group’s codes.

Open the BpS raster’s attribute table.
Click Select By Attributes and build a query on BPS_NAME, e.g., BPS_NAME contains the text Spruce.
Note the distinct BPS_CODE values among the selected rows. Several rows may share one code; list each code once.
Record the codes in your worksheet.

Make the mask with Raster Calculator (Spatial Analyst), using Con and InList. Double-click bps_code in the Rasters list to insert it, then type the rest:
Con(InList("bps_code", [13651, 13652, 13653]), 1, 0)
Replace the codes with your group’s codes.

Output raster: gX_mask

Cells outside the BpS raster’s data area stay NoData; that is expected.
If InList is unavailable in your version, use Con(("bps_code" == 13651) | ("bps_code" == 13652), 1, 0), or Reclassify the group’s codes to 1 and all other codes to 0.

Aggregating converts 1/0 pixels into a share. For example, a 90 m cell containing 4 group pixels out of 9 gets a value of 0.44.
Aggregate (Spatial Analyst; see How Aggregate works)

Input raster: gX_mask
Output raster: gX_share
Cell factor: 3
Aggregation technique: Mean
Expand extent if needed: checked
Ignore NoData in calculations: checked (cells at the edge average only their valid pixels)

Then Raster Calculator:
Con(IsNull("gX_share"), 0, "gX_share")

Output raster: gX_sharez

Check: the output is floating point, ranging from 0 to 1, with a 90 m cell size (Properties > Source > Raster Information).



Each cell gets the average of itself and its 8 neighbors, so it now holds the group’s share of a 270 m × 270 m neighborhood.
Focal Statistics (Spatial Analyst; see How Focal Statistics works)

Input raster: gX_sharez
Output raster: gX_smooth
Neighborhood: Rectangle
Height: 3, Width: 3, Units type: Cell
Statistics type: Mean
Ignore NoData in calculations: checked

Check: values still range from 0 to 1, and the surface looks like a soft-focus version of gX_sharez.
Optional: extra passes. For rounder, simpler polygons, run Focal Statistics again with the same settings on gX_smooth, then contour that output instead. Each pass blurs a little more. Repeated averaging approaches a Gaussian blur; with 90 m cells, one pass blurs by about 73 m, two passes by about 104 m and three by about 127 m. One pass works well for most uses. When tested on a 1.5 million acre forest, two passes cut the polygon count by about 20% and changed total acres by less than 1%.



Contour (Spatial Analyst; see How Contouring works)

Input raster: gX_smooth
Output feature class: gX_bands
Contour interval: your contour level (e.g., 0.4)
Base contour: 0
Contour type: Contour polygon

The output is a set of non-overlapping bands: 0–0.4, 0.4–0.8 and 0.8 up to the maximum. Setting the interval equal to the level guarantees a band boundary exactly at the level.
Keep the bands at or above the level:

Open the attribute table of gX_bands. It has fields holding each band’s lower and upper contour values; field names vary by Pro version.

Input features: gX_bands
Output feature class: gX_contour
Dissolve fields: none
Create multipart features: checked

This merges the selected bands into one feature: everywhere the neighborhood share is at least the level.

Alternative: Contour shell up returns overlapping “shells”, each running from a contour value up to the raster maximum. Keep the shell whose lower value equals your level, and delete the rest.

Output feature class: gX_clip

Input features: gX_clip
Output feature class: gX_single

Input features: gX_single
Output feature class: gX_simple
Simplification algorithm: Retain critical points (Douglas-Peucker)
Simplification tolerance: e.g., 15 Meters

Field
Type

Picture a strip where pine and hemlock pixels are interspersed: after smoothing, the pine polygon and the hemlock polygon both cover the strip. If both were mapped, that strip would be counted twice in acreage totals, and the map would show two colors stacked on each other.
The rule. Each overlap goes to the higher-priority group. For each group, erase every area already covered by any higher-priority group. Group 1 keeps everything; group 2 loses what overlaps group 1; group 3 loses what overlaps groups 1 or 2; and so on.

Output feature class: g3_final

import arcpy

arcpy.env.workspace = r"C:\path\to\YourProject.gdb"  # EDIT: geodatabase with the gX_simple layers
arcpy.env.overwriteOutput = True

# EDIT: one entry per group, highest priority first
simple = ["g1_simple", "g2_simple", "g3_simple", "g4_simple"]

for k, fc in enumerate(simple, start=1):
    out = f"g{k}_final"
    if k == 1:
        arcpy.management.CopyFeatures(fc, out)
    elif k == 2:

    else:

        arcpy.management.Merge(simple[:k - 1], above)
        arcpy.analysis.PairwiseErase(fc, above, out)
    print(out, arcpy.management.GetCount(out)[0], "polygons")

title: Smoothed Biophysical Settings polygons in ArcGIS Pro
text:
Rounder, simpler shapes: add a second or third blur pass (step 4).
Capture narrow or scattered patches: lower the contour level (e.g., 0.35). Expect polygons to grow into neighboring types.
Group-specific settings: each group can use its own contour level or number of passes. Scattered types benefit from a lower contour level and a single pass.
Map scale:

Small areas or large-scale maps: use a smaller minimum size, and possibly no aggregation (cell factor 1, so the blur works on 30 m cells; slower).
Regional extents: use a larger aggregation factor or more blur passes.

Simplify tolerance: keep it well below the cell size so shapes stay rounded. Increase it only if file size matters (e.g., web maps).

title: Smoothed Biophysical Settings polygons in ArcGIS Pro
text:
Not current vegetation: BpS represents vegetation that may have been dominant prior to Euro-American settlement. Smoothed BpS polygons do not map current vegetation.
Edges are approximate: polygon edges are the chosen neighborhood-share line, not an observed boundary. Use the polygons for planning-scale display and screening, not site-level decisions.
Software differences: results from ArcGIS Pro and other software (e.g., the R terra + isoband equivalent) differ slightly because contour interpolation and simplification algorithms differ. Expect differences of a few percent in acres.

title: Smoothed Biophysical Settings polygons in ArcGIS Pro
text:
Decide which BpSs to map and how to group them. A group can be a single BpS or several related ones (e.g., all spruce-fir variants). For each group, record:

Group name
BPS_CODE values in the group. Use BPS_CODE, not the raster VALUE: one BpS code can have several raster values (map zone variants), and the group should include all of them. Step 2 explains how to find the codes. Read the BpS model descriptions to decide which BpSs belong together.
Priority, if mapping more than one group. Groups are smoothed independently, so their edges can overlap; overlaps go to the higher-priority group (step 9). Putting rarer or more important groups first keeps them from being swallowed by widespread neighbors.
Color. The colorblind-safe Okabe-Ito palette works well: #0072B2, #F0E442, #56B4E9, #009E73, #CC79A7, #E69F00, #D55E00, #000000. Leave a few colors unused if other layers will be drawn on top.

title: Smoothed Biophysical Settings polygons in ArcGIS Pro
text:
Visual check: zoom into a few areas with the raw BpS raster (group pixels highlighted) under the polygon outlines. Edges should follow the bulk of the pixels without stair steps.
Acreage check: compare each group’s smoothed acres to its raw pixel acres.

Smoothed acres: select the group in bps_smooth and look at the statistics of acres. Alternatively, run Summary Statistics with acres SUM and case field group.
Raw acres: the number of group pixels × 0.2224 acres for 30 m cells. Get the pixel count from the COUNT field of the BpS attribute table (summed over the group’s rows) or from Tabulate Area.

How to read the ratio of smoothed to raw acres:

Roughly 90–110%: typical for widespread groups that occur in large patches.
Well above 100%: the contour is absorbing neighboring types in mixed areas. Raise the contour level.
Well below 100%: the group occurs as small or scattered patches that fall below the contour level or the minimum size. Lower the contour level or the minimum size, if those patches matter.

Overlaps: see the check at the end of step 9.

title: Smoothed Biophysical Settings polygons in ArcGIS Pro
text:
The kernel is a normalized 2-D Gaussian extending 3 sigma from the center (about 99% of a Gaussian’s weight lies within 3 sigma). It is the same as terra::focalMat(r, sigma, "Gauss") in R. The file format is described under “Weight” in How Focal Statistics works.
Run this in the ArcGIS Pro Python window or any Python with numpy. Set cell_m to the cell size after aggregation:
import numpy as np

def write_gauss_kernel(path, sigma_m, cell_m):
    half = int(np.floor(3 * sigma_m / cell_m))
    d = np.arange(-half, half + 1) * cell_m
    x, y = np.meshgrid(d, d)
    w = np.exp(-(x**2 + y**2) / (2 * sigma_m**2))
    w = w / w.sum()
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        f.write(f"{w.shape[1]} {w.shape[0]}\n")
        for row in w:
            f.write(" ".join(f"{v:.8f}" for v in row) + "\n")

write_gauss_kernel(r"C:\path\to\gauss_kernel_90m_sigma100.txt", sigma_m=100, cell_m=90)
The first line of the file is the kernel width and height in cells; the following lines are the weights, row by row. ArcGIS requires a .txt extension and no spaces in the file name.

title: Smoothed Biophysical Settings polygons in ArcGIS Pro
text:
Create a project. Open ArcGIS Pro and start a new project from the Map template. Pro creates a project file geodatabase (YourProject.gdb). Save every output there unless told otherwise; geodatabases handle long field names and large polygons better than shapefiles.
Add data. On the Map tab, click Add Data and add the BpS raster and the boundary polygon.
Check the BpS attribute table. In the Contents pane, right-click the BpS raster and choose Attribute Table. You should see VALUE, BPS_CODE, BPS_NAME and other fields. If only VALUE and COUNT are present, the attributes were lost (this can happen after clipping). Use Join Field to bring them back from the CSV attribute table that comes with the LANDFIRE download, joining on VALUE.
Trim the raster if it is much larger than your area. If the BpS raster covers a whole region or the country, use Clip Raster to cut it to your boundary’s extent plus a buffer of about 1 km. The buffer lets polygons at the edge “see” real neighbors during the blur; the polygons are clipped to the exact boundary later (step 7).
Set environments. On the Analysis tab, click Environments and set:

Output Coordinate System: a projected system in meters. Choosing Same as Input with the BpS raster’s projection (NAD 1983 Contiguous USA Albers, EPSG 5070, for CONUS LANDFIRE) works. Avoid geographic (degrees) coordinates; areas and distances would be wrong.
Processing Extent: same as the BpS raster.
Snap Raster: the BpS raster. This keeps every raster output aligned to the same grid.
Leave Mask empty. Cells outside the boundary need to be 0, not NoData, for the blur (handled in step 3).

See Geoprocessing environment settings for details.




Open a tool: on the Analysis tab, click Tools. In the Geoprocessing pane, search for the tool by name, fill in the parameters and click Run.
Check results: a green banner means success. Click View Details to see warnings; some are harmless, but read them.
Rerun with different inputs: on the Analysis tab, click History. Double-click a previous run to reopen the tool with the same settings, then change the inputs and output names. This is the fastest way to repeat steps 2–8 for each group (Geoprocessing history).
Automating: steps 2–8 can be chained in ModelBuilder, with the group codes and name as model parameters. Steps 9 and 11 include Python you can paste into the Python window (Analysis tab > Python > Python Window).
